title: Monitoring Daytime Differences in Exercise Capacity Using Treadmill Test and Muscle Dissection
author: Adamovich, Ezagouri, et al.

steps.title: Define moderate intensity parameters
steps.instruction: Set moderate intensity as 45–75% of maximal running capacity, which corresponds to approximately 60% of the maximal velocity (Vmax). For untrained C57BL/6J mice (average Vmax ≈ 40 cm/s), this translates to a constant treadmill speed of 22–25 cm/s.

steps.title: Record body weight and match cohorts
steps.instruction: Weigh each mouse and select weight‑matched animals; record all body‑weight values for later analysis.

steps.title: Set treadmill and lighting conditions
steps.instruction: Program the treadmill to run at the defined speed of 22–25 cm/s (no slope specified). Document the light‑dark cycle (e.g., 12 h light – 12 h dark) and note the experiment start time using Zeitgeber time (ZT).

steps.title: Run mice continuously until fatigue
steps.instruction: Place the mice on the treadmill and run them continuously for several hours (duration varies with time of day) until fatigue is observed (mouse can no longer maintain the set speed despite motivation).

steps.title: Document run outcomes
steps.instruction: Record the total run duration, the exact ZT at which the run started and ended, the speed used (22–25 cm/s), and the fatigue point for each mouse.

description: Here we detail a protocol that applies a constant running speed at a moderate intensity, which is often referred to as “endurance running.” Endurance running, or long-distance running, is a type of exercise that involves aerobic metabolism. The running intensity is defined by the speed and slope that corresponds to the “aerobic power” needed. A moderate intensity run is often considered as 45%–75% of the maximal running capacity (Hawley et al., 2014). To determine the maximum power, you need to perform a treadmill test together with gas analyzer equipment and obtain the VO2max/VO2peak (Hoydal et al., 2007; Petrosino et al., 2016). A simpler, yet less accurate, alternative is to do an incremental speed test until mice cannot run anymore and obtain the maximum velocity (Vmax), which correlates with VO2max/VO2peak (Jordan et al., 2017; Picoli et al., 2018) . In this protocol we use a speed of 22–25 cm/s which is considered as moderate intensity (within ∼60% of their maximal velocity), as untrained C57BL/6J mice reach a Vmax on average at 40 cm/s (Ezagouri et al., 2019). The moderate intensity running session lasts a few hours, depending on the time of the day, until animals reach fatigue (see below).Note: the duration of this protocol is different than an acceleration speed protocol that lasts a few minutes, until mice are unable to maintain the elevated running speed and increased workload, which is accompanied by elevated blood lactate levels, and often referred to as “run to exhaustion.”CRITICAL: As oxygen and energy needs differ relative to body size and composition, make sure you record the bodyweights in your study and preferably use weight-matched animals.
